en: In the past, the World-Honored One entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa, with Ānanda as his deputy to transmit and transform others so that it would not be severed. This continued until the Five Houses emerged with their distinct proclamations, whereby the style of our school pervaded the ten directions. Yet, even Huangbo still harbored the lament: "There is no lack of Chan; there is only a lack of teachers. Why was this?

At that time, the young Linji alone attained the function of the Great Capacity; he was accustomed to stroking a tiger’s whiskers and acted with total authority. The people of the great earth were left speechless, their tongues tied by his sharp wit. Huangbo recorded that when our school reached [Linji]...

You have brought great flourishing to the world. Although there was a convergence of causes and conditions, your function was nonetheless distinct and transcendent. Subsequently, heroic spirits arose one after another, each like a lion cub; mountain ghosts and wild foxes fled at the mere sound of the wind.

Thus, the Eye of the True Dharma has been transmitted down to the present day, which is why those who understand it acknowledge the subtlety of the Master’s lineage. The fundamental principles of the Cao-Dong school for discerning demons and distinguishing the heterodox are, in their general purport, largely the same as those of Linji. Therefore, the propagation of this Dharma path began and ended alongside that of Linji.

However, from Dayang onwards, when Touzi succeeded him, the Cao-Dong school also branched out from Linji. An ancient said, "They unite for five hundred years and then separate; they separate for five hundred years and then unite. Might this indeed be so? Thus, from the end of the Song dynasty...

In our Ming dynasty, there were heroic and eminent masters; yet their fragmented records and broken scrolls have been lost amidst the wild thickets and withered weeds. Alas, it is tragic that the descendants of later generations desire to know their names but cannot find them.

Master Mǐn of Mount Lú was a high-ranking disciple of Great Master Tiāntóng. He extensively collected inscriptions and biographies, arranging them into a comprehensive compilation. From Mount Língshān down to Cáoqī, thirty-three generations had already passed; from below Cáoqī down to Yǔmén, another thirty-three generations had passed. The succession from beginning to end is as seamless as two halves of a tally.

With Tiāntóng arising in the interim, the flourishing of the lineage is truly far from over. Tiāntóng wielded a single white staff to test all quarters; whether a Buddha or a Patriarch came, he would strike them across the spine without hesitation.

Even with supernatural powers and wondrous functions, there is nowhere to hide; the Linji school has flourished greatly in the world—how marvelous! Initially, when I served Shouchang, I consulted him for the longest time, yet I still regretted that I had left my teacher too early and failed to fully grasp his excellence.

Later, while attending the Great Master again at Tiantong, I beheld his dynamic pedagogical methods and only then marveled that the spirit of Linji still endured. Shouchang once told me: "When I was fifty years old, I traveled to follow the Dharma at Rui Feng, though I did not get to know in detail whose lineage Rui Feng belonged to.

I examined the *Chanzeng shipei* (Genealogy of the Chan Lamps) and found that Rui Feng originally shared the same master as Yumen; thus, Shouchang was indeed a direct descendant of the Linji bloodline. His succession of Lingshan and the renaming of the lineage as Caodong actually accords with the precedent set by Touzi.

The light of the sun and moon proceed together without conflict. It is surely the World-Honored One’s entrustment that we, as his deputies, shall transmit and transform [the Dharma], ensuring it does not cease for those yet to come.

Written on the third day of the third month in the fifth year of the Chongzhen era, by the disciple Huang Duober, with prostrations and reverence, as the postscript to the *Chan Deng Shi Pu* (Genealogy of the Lamp of Chan).

The transmission of my ancestors' Way to the various states of the Central Plains began in the Liang dynasty, flourished in the Tang, and reached its zenith of glory in the Song. During these periods, there were frequently many scholars of lofty writings and vast erudition;

thus, the life and career of our late virtuous predecessor, as well as the general outlines of his words and deeds, all have biographical records for consultation, not merely genealogical registers. From the Yuan dynasty onwards, however, the transmission of the Lamp was neglected, which resulted in the fact that a master of a generation and those who followed his footsteps on Mount Xishan were equally submerged and forgotten. How truly lamentable this is!

When I, Meng, first tasted the flavor of the Dharma upon entering the monastic order, I was struck with a profound sense of regret and resolved to pursue the path of the unofficial historians and folk chroniclers. However, as inscriptions were ruined and manuscripts were lost, there was nothing to be gathered; thus, I intended to consult the genealogical charts of our school to compile a secular lineage history (*shipei*) to fulfill that ambition. Just as I had begun this preliminary work, it remained unfinished.

When the Elder Jin-su received an invitation from Huangbo, he entered Min as his attendant. There, I obtained the compilation by Mr. Wu; my own prior intentions coincided with his without prior consultation. However, I regretted that it contained many errors, omissions, and forced associations, inevitably falling into the fault of failing to inspire confidence due to a lack of evidence.

Consequently, I consulted the *Tripiṭaka* and various records of the *Lamp of the Dharma* (*Fozu Tongji*), selecting only those accounts of spiritual lineage for which there was reliable documentation. I did not dare to include anything based on mere hearsay or conjecture to confuse future generations.

As for those who preached the Dharma in their time but whose succession remains unclear, I have merely appended them to the end of their respective schools, awaiting further details to supplement the record. Thus, having verified the text through careful collation and substantiated it with historical testimony, I hope it may gain the trust of the future. This is but one small aid toward attaining the reality behind the names. May future gentlemen... [The text ends here.]
Regarding those who follow and transmit the Lamp, it may be that some will examine and verify this genealogy; this remains to be seen.

A Genealogical Chart of the Thirty-three Patriarchs.
The Primal Ancestor Śākyamuni Buddha (also known as Śākyamuni Buddha) is the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa.

He manifested his birth in the kingdom of Madhyadeśa in Central India, belonging to the Kṣatriya caste; Śākya was his clan name. His father was King Śuddhodana, and his mother was Queen Māyā. He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin, the ninth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.

Having renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he left the household life, realized the Unsurpassed Way, and turned the Great Dharma Wheel. Later, at the age of seventy-nine, as he was about to enter Parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Great Dharma Seal to Mahākāśyapa.

In the thirty-sixth year of King Mu, on the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Renshen, he entered parinirvāṇa at midnight. One thousand and seventeen years later, the teaching reached the Middle Kingdom; this was precisely the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han, the year of Dingmao.

According to the various records of the *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), the seven Buddhas are recorded first, followed by the successive patriarchs. However, the *Dongshan chuanfa zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Dharma Transmission of Dongshan) maintains that the orthodox lineage must be verified through direct face-to-face transmission; therefore, it takes Śākyamuni Buddha as the founding patriarch.

Mahākāśyapa was the first patriarch. Reaching down to the world of the Sixth Patriarch Dajian of Caoxi, the succession was inherited in turn. This is intended to clarify the great outline of the transformation through the Single Buddha Vehicle and the fundamental source of the successive patriarchs who transmitted the essence.
Therefore, this genealogical chart does not include the seven Buddhas, but instead takes Śākyamuni Buddha as the founding ancestor.
(First Patriarch) Mahākāśyapa was a native of Magadha. He was of Brahmin descent;
his father was named Āṅgirasa and his mother was named Gāndhārī. Previously...
He left his home to enter the mountains and cultivated himself through the dhūta practices.
Encountering the Buddha, he left the household life and received the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which was subsequently entrusted to Ānanda. Thus...
Carrying the fly-whisk and the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe entrusted to him,
he entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
this was during the reign of King Zhou Xiao.
(Second Patriarch) Venerable Ānanda was of the Kṣatriya caste.
He was the son of King Droṇodana and the younger cousin of the Buddha.
He was profoundly learned and widely erudite.
He was foremost in dhāraṇī; he compiled all the Sūtra-piṭaka.
When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to his disciple Śāṇavāsa.
Furthermore, that Nāga Āśvina entrusted [the teachings] to Madhyāntika,
who entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of King Zhouyi.
The Third Patriarch, Śaṇakavāsin, was a native of the country of Tuḷuḷa. His clan name was Viśākha;
his father was Linsheng, and his mother was Qiūshēyē.
He remained in the womb for six years.
At birth, he was naturally clothed in garments that grew with his body.
He left the household life as a disciple of Ānanda and received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.
After dwelling at the Uruvilvā monastery and subduing the two fire-dragons,
he entrusted the Dharma to Upagupta and entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of King Xuan of the Zhou dynasty.
(The Fourth Patriarch) Upagupta was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā.
His clan name was Śūdra, his father’s name was Sumati,
and he left the household life to attain the Way.
His traces were extraordinary; he was titled the Buddha Without Marks.
He subdued the Māra Pāpīyas and delivered the greatest number of people;
those whom he predicted for enlightenment filled the counting sticks to overflowing.
In the reign of King Ping of the Zhou dynasty, he entered parinirvāṇa at the Stone Chamber.
His disciple Toku-shi cremated the chamber using counting sticks,
collected the relics, and erected a stūpa.
(The Fifth Patriarch) Diṭṭhagga was a native of Magadha.
His father dreamed of a golden sun before his birth. He encountered the Venerable Upāli.
To explain the meaning of his dream, he received the True Dharma and later entrusted it to Mijia (Mecaka).
He then transformed himself into fire and incinerated his own body;
this was during the reign of King Zhuang of Zhou.
(The Sixth Patriarch) Micaka was a native of Central India.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Northern India,
he saw a golden [light] amidst the city battlements.
Ruìyún said, "This is the aura of the Mahāyāna.
Having met Vāsumitra, he was entrusted with the Dharma;
during the reign of King Xiang of the Zhou dynasty, he transformed himself into fire and self-immolated."
(Seventh Patriarch) Vāsumitra was a native of Northern India. His family name was Bharadvāja.
He traveled to the country of Kāmarūpa to propagate the Dharma.
He subdued Buddhadeva through debate and entrusted him with the True Dharma.
During the reign of King Zhouding, he passed away at his seat;
his entire body was enshrined in a stupa.
(8th Patriarch) Buddhanandi was a native of the country of Kāmala. His clan name was Gautama.
He was born with a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown. By nature...
He was of great intelligence, possessing swift and unimpeded eloquence.
During the reign of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty,
he entrusted the Dharma to Puṇyamitra and entered a solemn state of parinirvāṇa.
(The Ninth Patriarch) Vṛddhamitra was a native of the country of Tiqia. His clan name was Viśāla.
He was born unable to speak. [He was the teacher of] Venerable Nanti.
He revealed his past affinities and entrusted him with the seal of the Dharma.
Later, he obtained the son of the elder Gandhaka as a disciple.
He entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty.
(10th Patriarch) Venerable Pārśva was a native of Central India. His original name was Nan-sheng.
He practiced asceticism with such rigorous devotion that his side never touched the mat.
He traveled to the kingdom of Puṣpapura to convert beings, first manifesting auspicious signs.
He indeed received the Dharma-transmission from Yaśas;
when King Zhou Dingru ascended the throne, he converted the fire and immolated himself.
(The Eleventh Patriarch) Pūrṇaśa was a native of the country of Puṣpāvatī. His clan name was Gautama.
He traveled to the country of Vārāṇasī to propagate the teachings and attained [enlightenment].
The Great Being Ming was entrusted with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
during the reign of King Zhou’an, he passed away into profound stillness,
and his entire body was interred in a stupa.
(12th Patriarch) Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was a native of Vārāṇasī;
because his merit was exceptionally superior.
He also subdued Kāpila as his disciple and eventually entrusted the Dharma to him.
During the reign of King Xian of the Zhou dynasty, he entered great parinirvāṇa.
(Thirteenth Patriarch) Kāpimāla was a native of the country of Huashi.
Initially a follower of non-Buddhist paths,
he later received the Dharma from the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa.
He subdued the great fire-dragon and thereby took Nāgārjuna as his disciple,
entrusting him with the treasury of the True Dharma.
He entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of King Nan Wang of Zhou.
(14th Patriarch) Venerable Nāgārjuna was a native of Western India.
He composed numerous treatises at length to expound and clarify the True Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
It was appropriate that, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted his dharma-seal to Kāṇadeva during the era of the First Emperor of Qin.
(The Fifteenth Patriarch) Kanadeva was a native of South India. His family name was Viśeṣa.
He first went to visit Nāgārjuna, who [presented him with] a bowl.
He placed water in his seat; the Venerable One cast a needle into it, and they joyfully reached a state of spiritual resonance.
He entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of the Han dynasty.
(The Sixteenth Patriarch) Rāhulata was a native of Kāpiśī. His clan name was Guṇamati.
Having encountered Deva, he attained clarity.
Due to the circumstance of [the Buddha] growing ears like trees at home,
he subsequently left the household life and received the Great Dharma Seal. He entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty.
(Seventeenth Patriarch) Saṃghanandin was a native of Śrāvastī.
He was the son of Prince Ratnavyūha;
he was able to speak from birth and entered the monastic life.
He resided at the Golden River Grotto.
When Rāhulabhadra arrived there, he transmitted the essential teachings of the Great Dharma.
During the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Han dynasty, he passed away while grasping a tree with his hands.
(18th Patriarch) Gayasata was a native of Mathura. His clan name was Udraka;
his father was Deva-śila and his mother was Bhadra. She dreamed of a jewel...
From a mirror, a Great Being was born; his body was like lapis lazuli.
Encountering Nandika, he attained deliverance and received the Dharma.
During the reign of Emperor Cheng of the Han dynasty, he transformed himself into fire and self-immolated.
(19th Patriarch) Kumārajīva was a native of the Yuezhi people. As the son of a Brahmin,
he encountered the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, who entrusted him with the Dharma.
He then used his fingernails to scratch his face,
emitting a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly,
before entering into nirvana; this was during the era of Xing Mang.
(The Twentieth Patriarch) Jayata was a native of Northern India.
He encountered Kumāralāta and heard his teachings on the penetration of karma.
He attained realization across three lifetimes, left the household life, and attained the Dharma.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, he manifested a miraculous transformation by planting himself upside down and suddenly passing away.
(The Twenty-first Patriarch) Vāsukandra was a native of Rājagṛha.
Initially, he admired Kāśyapa and practiced the dhūta austerities. Because of the great darkness of night...
The Master stimulated his great wisdom and thereby received the transmission of the Dharma.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Later Han dynasty, he transcended his body and entered nirvana.
(The Twenty-second Patriarch) was Prince Sadāprarudita of the country of Maṇalānada.
He possessed great supernatural powers. His father appointed him as his teacher.
Xiu Pantou left the household life and received the transmission of the Dharma.
During the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty, he ascended into the great void and pointed his finger at the ground to cause a spring to gush forth;
thereafter, he entered a state of serene extinction.
(The Twenty-third Patriarch) Hegalena was a native of the country of Moji.
He was the son of a Brahmin and possessed extraordinary signs at birth.
Having left the household life, he devoted himself exclusively to recitation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was revealed to him, and he was moved by a flock of cranes that took refuge in it.
Later, he encountered Maṇḍarava and attained the Dharma.
He entered nirvana during the reign of Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty.

(The Twenty-fifth Patriarch) Vāsṣaṭa was a native of Kaśmīra.
He was of Brahmin lineage and possessed extraordinary signs at birth. He was the venerable Siṃha.
Having discerned his past affinity, he was entrusted with the robe of faith of the Great Dharma;
he subsequently transformed beings in Central India, South India, and the Southern Celestial Continent (Jambudvīpa).
He entered parinirvāṇa during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
(The Twenty-sixth Patriarch) Bodhidharma was the crown prince of King Deśeṇa in South India;
he left the household life under Vasiṣṭha.
The Transmission of the Dharma: During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin dynasty,
he entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Prajñātāra and then transformed himself into fire to immolate his own body.
(The Twenty-seventh Patriarch) Prajñātāra was a native of East India. Initially, as a youth,
he encountered Ratnamitra, who revealed his saintliness.
He subsequently left the household life to transmit the Dharma and traveled to teach and transform beings in South India,
where he received the transmission of the Dharma from Bodhidharma.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, he entered parinirvāṇa.
(28th Patriarch) Bodhidharma was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India;
He transmitted the Dharma within his own family, and his transformation reached the six schools;
his fame resounded throughout the five regions of India.
Sixty-seven years later, he brought the Dharma eastward to China.
He was the first patriarch in the Eastern Land;
in the ninth month of the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the year of Gengzi,
he crossed the sea and arrived at Guangzhou on the twenty-first day.
On the first day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Jianye.
Finding that his karmic conditions were not in accord with Emperor Wu,
he departed for Northern Wei and stayed at Mount Song and Mount Shao.
In his [fiftieth] year, he received the divine light;
standing in the snow, he severed his own arm, whereupon the Master revealed the essentials of the Dharma. Later, the robe and the Dharma were entrusted to him.
He then suddenly passed away, during the Liang dynasty.

Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. His mother was surnamed Zhou.
He was born with the marks of a great man,
yet he fell short of the Tathāgata in seven respects. At the age of seven,
he encountered the Great Master, entered the monastic life, and immediately received his teachings.
He subsequently resided at Mount Pòtóu, where his teaching flourished greatly.
In the second year of the Shàngyuán era of Emperor Gāozōng,
the year of Yǐhài, he entered nirvana at the age of seventy-four.

Qingyuan Xingsi was a native of Ancheng in Liu Province. He left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Jingju on Mount Qingyuan.
At the temple, he entered parinirvāṇa on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month in the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong.
His posthumous title was Hongji, and his stupa was named Guizhen. His lineage is recorded separately.

According to the various patriarchs of the Western lands at the time of their parinirvāṇa, the *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp) all records them by correlating them with the cyclical years of the Zhou and Qin dynasties. However, the *Zheng zong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) states that China and India are separated by tens of thousands of li;

when these individuals passed away, some were even more than a thousand years later. Their affairs are thus remote and distant. I fear that by comparing them through multiple translations, it would not be easy to obtain the actual facts. Therefore, I have briefly omitted the specific years and *jiazi* cycles, and shall instead preserve only the imperial reigns.

This applies to all except for Śākyamuni Buddha and the six patriarchs from Bodhidharma down to our arrival in China, whose years of entry and parinirvāṇa can be somewhat inferred and verified, and thus may be recorded in full. Now, I follow this approach.

The Stele Inscription composed by the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) Qiu Xuansu states:
"The Chan Master was a native of Zhugong. His surname was Cui, and he was a descendant of the Yu lineage.
At the age of fifteen, he entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Tanchu of Changsha Temple."
At thirty-three, he went to Gao-shan to receive the precepts. At thirty, he attended Shitou and repeatedly received his instructions, yet he had never yet grasped the essential point.
Next, he visited National Teacher Zhong. At thirty-four, together with National Teacher’s attendant Yingzhen, he returned south to visit Mazu.
Mazu said, "Recognize your own mind; it is originally Buddha and does not belong to the gradual path."

Next, there was no need for further cultivation; his essence was naturally suchness (*tathatā*), and he was fully endowed with all virtues. Upon hearing these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
The Patriarch instructed him, saying, "If you take up the position of abbot, do not leave your former location.

Having received this guidance, the Master returned to Jingmen. Not far from the city walls, he thatched together grass to form a hut. Later, when the regional commander inquired of his attendants, [he learned of the Master's presence].
He set forth the details of the matter. A regional inspector personally visited to seek the Way;

seeing that the path was so narrow that carriages and horses could not pass, and observing that the surrounding wilderness had never been cleared or trimmed, he grew enraged at this sight. He ordered his men to seize the Master and cast him into the water.
Just as the banners and pennants were returning, they saw fire break out throughout the entire administrative office, with great flames raging both inside and out, impossible to extinguish.
He drew near, hearing only a voice from the air saying, "I am the deity Tianwang Shen. The regional inspector turned his heart toward repentance and prostrated himself;

the flames and smoke were instantly extinguished, and everything was restored as it had been before. He then went to the riverbank and saw the Master standing in the water without his robes being wet at all.
The regional inspector again offered a full confession and invited him to the prefectural office to receive offerings in the western part of the administration building.
He built a temple, which was named T'ien-wang-ssu (Temple of the Heavenly King). He used to say constantly, "How happy! How happy!
Yet when his end approached, he cried out, "Suffering! Suffering! and said, "The King of Yama has come to take me.
The head of the monastery asked him, "When you were previously thrown into the water by the Military Commissioner, your countenance remained unmoved; how can you now act like this?"
"Mo-di. The Master raised his meditation pillow and said, "Tell me, was it like this at that time, or is it like this now?

The head monk had no reply and immediately passed away. This occurred on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the third year of the Yuanhe era (the Wuzi year), at the age of eighty-two, having spent sixty-three summer retreats in seated meditation.

According to various records in the *Chuan deng lu*, there was an error in identifying Emperor-Tianhuang Daowu as Tianwang Daowu; consequently, Longtan and Deshan were categorized under the lineage of Qingyuan. Those with discernment doubted this. Later, the discovery of the stele inscriptions by Regional Inspector Qiu Xuansu and Court Musician Fu Zai sufficiently corrected these errors.

However, the epitaph for Chan Master Xuedou Xian, composed by Lü Xiāngqīng—who held the rank of Zhí bìgé—is even more explicit. It states in brief: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was bestowed by the Buddha upon Mahākāśyapa, and the transmission of the Saṃghāṭī robe served as a token for those destined to succeed him in appearing in the world to achieve enlightenment.

From that time on, the robe and the Dharma were transmitted together through twenty-seven generations. [The robe] reached Prince Simha, who first entered China and was posthumously titled Yuánjué (Perfect Enlightenment). Yuánjué transmitted it to Dàzǔ (the Great Patriarch), and Dàzǔ transmitted it to..."

Jianzhi transmitted [the lineage] to Dayi; Dayi transmitted it to Daman; Daman transmitted it to Dajian. Dajian merely stored away his robe and transmitted the Dharma. Dahui succeeded him, and Daishi inherited it.

Thereafter, they were all designated by the names of their residences—such as Tianwang, Longtan, Deshan, Xuefeng, Yunmen, Xianglin, and Zhimen—which represent their chronological succession. The Chan Master’s name was Chongxian, with the style name Yinzhi; he was the ninth-generation descendant of Daishi and the Dharma heir of Zhimen.
Based on this, the errors in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) become self-evident. Therefore, this genealogical chart has been specifically corrected accordingly.
